beginner: The economy grew 2.2% last quarter, which means businesses and workers are still making progress even though the geopolitical shock from the Iran war is pressuring energy prices.
Growth at 2.2% sits right around the Fed's estimate of what the economy can sustain without overheating, so the economy is neither racing ahead nor stalling out.
Watch whether the next quarter's number stays near 2% or starts to slip, because energy prices from the Iran conflict could slow consumer spending if they keep rising.
moderate: The economy expanded 2.2% against a backdrop of the Fed holding rates at 3.25%, which is restrictive enough to cool demand but not so tight that it crushes growth outright.
This pace matches historical post-pandemic norms (2-2.5%), unlike 2024 when growth ran hotter and forced the Fed to rethink its rate cuts.
If the Iran war pushes oil above $100/barrel sustained, watch for Q2 GDP to decelerate because consumers cut spending on non-energy goods when fuel costs spike.
expert: Real GDP growth of 2.2% annualized masks divergence: labor income remains solid but business fixed investment (ex-tech) has slowed from 3.8% in 2024 to 2.1% YTD, signaling caution from corporates on capex given geopolitical tail risk.

The Fed's March projections expected full-year 2026 growth near 2%, so the current run-rate aligns with their terminal assumptions, but energy supply shocks could push Q2-Q3 lower if oil shock persists.

Monitor the quarterly print's detail: if consumption drops while inventory investment swells, it signals demand rollover rather than sustainable growth, which would force the Fed to cut rates faster than currently priced.

beginner: Inflation just hit 2.3%, which is close to where the Fed wants it, but energy prices from the Iran war are still pushing upward so the next few months could surprise higher.

The Fed thought inflation would peak at 2.75-3% in the first half of 2026, and we are tracking below that today, but the OECD warns full-year inflation could land at 4.2% if the energy shock doesn't ease.
If gas prices stay elevated or rise further in the next month, the 2.3% we see now could jump back toward 3%, and the Fed will have to decide whether to hold rates steady or act.
moderate: Core inflation (ex-food and energy) has held in the 2.1-2.2% range for three months, suggesting underlying demand is cool, but headline CPI at 2.3% is being held down by a low base effect from 2025 energy weakness.

The Iran conflict reopened oil risk premium that markets had priced out in early 2026, and if Brent crude stays above $85-90/barrel, energy's drag on YoY inflation comparisons will flip to a boost by Q3.

Compare to 2022 when energy drove CPI to 9.1% and the Fed hiked 425 basis points: today's 3.25% rate and 2.3% CPI means real rates sit positive at ~0.95%, so the Fed has real policy room if energy shocks require action.
expert: CPI at 2.3% masks composition risk: core services inflation at 3.2% is sticky and labor-cost-driven, while goods deflation (-0.8% YoY) is fading as supply chains tighten on Iran-related logistics delays.

The Fed's terminal rate is 2.5% (neutral), and at 3.25% the policy rate is 75 basis points restrictive, but if oil breaches $100/barrel sustained and pushes headline CPI to 3.5%+ by May, expectations could de-anchor and force a hawkish hold or hike.

Watch the April CPI print (release date May 14) for energy base effects and shelter deceleration momentum; if both persist as tailwinds, the Fed can cut in June; if energy reignites, expect a pause through Q2.

beginner: The jobless rate sits at 4.2%, which is close to the Fed's estimate of full employment, so employers are still hiring but at a measured pace.
With unemployment holding steady, wage growth remains solid enough to keep consumers spending, even as the Iran war creates uncertainty about energy prices.
If unemployment starts to rise above 4.5% in the coming months, that would signal the economy is weakening, and the Fed would likely start cutting rates to support jobs.
moderate: Unemployment at 4.2% has been range-bound since late 2024 (4.1-4.3%), and the Fed's March projections kept it near 4.1-4.2% through 2026, meaning labor demand has found an equilibrium with supply.
Quits rate and job openings have both fallen from 2023 peaks, so the tight labor market of 2021-2022 has cooled into a balanced market where neither workers nor employers have acute leverage.

If energy shocks force businesses to cut capex (as noted above), watch for layoffs to cluster in discretionary sectors (retail, hospitality) in Q2-Q3, which could push unemployment above 4.5% and trigger Fed rate cuts.
expert: U-3 unemployment at 4.2% sits 15 basis points above the Fed's estimated natural rate (NAIRU of 4.05%), confirming the labor market is slightly loose; U-6 (underemployment) at 7.8% signals available slack for wage disinflation.

Labor force participation at 62.9% has stabilized after pandemic drift, but if geopolitical risk triggers a pullback in business formation, new entrants to the labor force could face weaker hiring, raising cyclical unemployment without spike in headline U-3.

The policy path depends on this metric: if unemployment edges above 4.5% in April-May payrolls, the Fed will cut in June; if it stays 4.0-4.3%, the Fed holds through Q2 and watches inflation before deciding Q3 moves.

beginner: The U.S. government is spending 6.9% more than it brings in each year, which means it is borrowing heavily to fund programs and defense, and that borrowing pushes up interest rates.
A deficit this large is unsustainable over decades, but in the short term it props up growth by putting money into the economy when private spending is soft.

Watch whether Congress tackles this problem in 2026-2027, because if the deficit stays above 6.5% of GDP for another two years, foreign investors may demand higher returns on U.S. bonds and the dollar could weaken.
moderate: The budget deficit at 6.9% of GDP is elevated compared to the pre-pandemic norm of 2-4%, and it reflects higher defense spending (Iran war preparedness), tax revenue shortfalls, and entitlement growth.

The Federal Reserve's balance sheet is shrinking (quantitative tightening), so the private sector must absorb more Treasury issuance; combined with a 6.9% deficit, this crowds out private investment and may explain why business capex has slowed.

Compare to 2023 when the deficit was 5.5% of GDP: the 140 basis point deterioration in two years is driven by geopolitical spending and weaker revenue growth, and it requires the 10Y bond yield to stay elevated (currently 4.42%) to attract buyers.
expert: The unified budget deficit of 6.9% of GDP is the third largest since 2000 (after 2009 and 2020), and primary deficit (ex-interest) sits at 4.1%, meaning interest expense is now 2.8% of GDP and crowding out discretionary spending.

CBO long-term projections (pre-March 2026) showed deficits structurally above 5% through 2030 due to aging and interest costs; if 10Y rates remain above 4% (currently 4.42%), interest service accelerates and forces either tax hikes or spending cuts by 2028.

Watch the April Treasury refunding announcement for issuance volume and maturity mix; if the deficit remains 6.5%+ through Q2, expect more long-duration supply (10Y/30Y weighted heavy), which could push yields higher and tighten financial conditions further.

beginner: America imports far more goods and services than it exports, running a deficit of 3.7% of GDP, which means the country is borrowing from foreigners to fund its consumption.
This deficit is partly because U.S. consumers and businesses buy cheap goods from overseas, and partly because the dollar is strong and makes American exports less competitive.
The current account deficit must be funded by foreign investment in U.S. assets, so if overseas investors lose confidence in the U.S., capital could dry up and the dollar would fall sharply.
moderate: The current account deficit at 3.7% of GDP is narrower than the 4.3% average of 2022-2023, thanks to weaker import demand and some export strength, but it remains elevated by historical standards (pre-2000 average was near zero).

The deficit is financed by capital inflows (foreign purchases of Treasury bonds, corporate equity, and real estate), and those inflows have held despite higher U.S. rates, signaling that U.S. assets still offer relative safety and returns.

The Iran war creates tail risk: if energy prices spike and import bills for oil surge, the current account deficit could widen back toward 4% unless exporters respond with stronger overseas sales, which is unlikely given global growth slowdown.
expert: The current account deficit of 3.7% of GDP masks sectoral divergence: goods deficit sits at 5.2% (durable goods imports from China/Vietnam remain resilient) while services surplus at 1.6% reflects U.S. dominance in software, finance, and media.

The deficit is financed by 2.1% of GDP in direct investment inflows and 1.8% in portfolio flows, but portfolio stability depends on the 10Y yield staying above 4%; if rates fall below 3.8% (Fed cut scenario), capital flows reverse and the dollar depreciates.

Monitor Q2 trade data (May 29 release) for import surge due to Iran oil premium: if petroleum imports jump 15-20% YoY in price, the goods deficit widens to 5.5%+, requiring either faster service export growth or capital flow acceleration to finance, both unlikely.

beginner: The Federal Reserve has interest rates set at 3.25%, which is above what economists think is normal, so borrowing is expensive for businesses and consumers.
The Fed hiked rates aggressively from 2022-2023 to fight inflation, and it has held steady since December 2023 because inflation has come down but not yet hit the 2% target.

Watch the Fed's June and September meetings in 2026: if inflation stays near 2.3% and unemployment stays near 4.2%, the Fed will likely start cutting rates to help the economy, which would lower mortgage and loan rates for everyone.
moderate: The policy rate at 3.25% is 75 basis points above the Fed's estimate of the neutral rate (2.5%), making monetary policy restrictive, but the Fed is holding here because it fears inflation could re-accelerate if it cuts too soon.

The Fed's March 2026 projections showed 75 basis points of rate cuts over 2026-2027 (to 2.5% by end-2027), but that forecast predated the full Iran war escalation and higher oil price expectations, so the committee may push cuts further out.

Compare to March 2022 when rates were near zero and inflation was rising: today's 3.25% is a hawkish stance by historical standards, and it is deliberately slowing credit growth and capex investment to cool demand.
expert: The real policy rate (3.25% minus 2.3% inflation) is 95 basis points restrictive, which exceeds the neutral real rate of 0.5-0.75% by 20-45 basis points, confirming financial conditions are tight and mortgage originations have fallen 35% YoY.

The FOMC's March dot plot showed median rate projections at 2.75% by year-end 2026 (100 bps of cuts from March), but recent inflation and geopolitical risk have pushed fed funds futures to price only 50 bps of cuts through December, a 50 bp repricing hawkish.

Watch the May FOMC meeting (May 6-7) for any hawkish shift in forward guidance; if officials acknowledge Iran energy risk persisting and inflation risks rising, expect the dot plot in June to show fewer cuts, which would steepen the yield curve (currently +82 bps) and support the dollar.

beginner: U.S. stocks are down 7.1% so far this year, which reflects worry about inflation staying higher due to the Iran war and concerns that the Fed will not cut rates as quickly as investors hoped.

Tech stocks have led the decline because they are most sensitive to interest rates: when borrowing costs rise or stay high, investors prefer safer assets, and the growth prospects of tech companies shrink.
If the Fed signals in the next few months that it will cut rates in the summer or fall, stock prices could rebound as cheaper borrowing would boost corporate earnings and valuations.
moderate: The stock market YTD return of negative 7.1% is driven by a 12-15% decline in mega-cap technology stocks (Magnificent Seven) and a smaller 2-3% decline in value and cyclical sectors that benefit from stable rates.

The decline mirrors a 40-50 basis point rise in the 10Y bond yield (from ~3.9% in early January to 4.42% today), which re-prices growth stock valuations lower; for every 50 bps of yield rise, growth stocks typically lose 4-6% of value.

Compare to 2024 when stocks rose 12% YTD despite higher rates, because earnings grew and investors extrapolated that momentum; today's decline reflects a loss of confidence in earnings growth and Fed rate cuts, a sentiment shift rather than pure yield impact.
expert: The S&P 500 YTD total return of negative 7.1% masks a 10-11% decline in the Magnificent Seven (NVIDIA, Tesla, Mag-7 equally weighted) and a positive 0.5% return in equal-weighted S&P 500, signaling factor concentration collapse and return of value.

The drawdown coincides with a repricing of 2026-2027 earnings expectations downward by 2-3% as energy cost pressures and capex caution spread; price-to-earnings multiple on the S&P 500 has compressed from 19.5x to 17.8x despite flattish earnings, indicating structural valuation pressure.

Monitor April earnings season (begins April 9): if revenue guidance flags due to Iran-related margin pressure or capex pullback, expect further 3-5% downside; if guidance holds and companies point to a summer stabilization, expect mean-reversion rally to reduce YTD loss to 2-3% by mid-May.

beginner: The yield on 10-year U.S. government bonds is 4.42%, which means investors demand nearly 4.5% annual return to lend to the U.S. for a decade, reflecting worry about inflation and budget deficits.

When bond yields rise, it makes mortgages, car loans, and corporate borrowing more expensive, which slows the economy, so the 4.42% yield is one reason stocks have fallen and consumers are spending cautiously.
If the Fed starts cutting rates later this year, bond yields will likely fall because investors will expect lower short-term rates and inflation, which would boost stocks and make borrowing cheaper.
moderate: The 10Y yield at 4.42% is 50-60 basis points higher than the Fed's policy rate (3.25%), which is a normal spread, but it reflects market expectations that inflation will stay above 2.5% over the next decade and that the Fed's neutral rate is higher than 2.5%.

The yield has risen 50 basis points since early January 2026 (from ~3.9%) as the Iran war reshuffled expectations for oil prices and inflation, and as the Treasury has been forced to issue more debt (6.9% deficit) to attract buyers.

Compare to mid-2024 when the 10Y was near 4%, then dropped to 3.7% by December as disinflation momentum built: today's 4.42% reflects reversal of that trade and re-concentration of tail risk in energy markets.
expert: The 10Y yield of 4.42% implies a real yield of 212 basis points (4.42 minus 2.3% inflation) and an inflation breakeven of 230 basis points, suggesting market pricing of average inflation at 2.3% over the next decade; this is 30-50 bps above the Fed's 2% target.

The 10Y-2Y spread at 82 basis points reflects both yield curve normalization (inversion has unwound) and term premium re-pricing: if the Fed cuts by 75 bps over 2026-2027 as currently priced, the 2Y moves down faster than the 10Y, and the curve steepens further to 120-140 bps.

Watch for policy shift at the May FOMC: if hawkish guidance emerges on inflation and energy, expect the 10Y to gap higher to 4.6-4.8% and trigger a broader re-pricing of risk assets; if dovish, expect a rapid decline to 4.1% and 200+ bp rally in long-duration growth stocks.

beginner: The yield curve, which measures the gap between long-term and short-term interest rates, is now at plus 82 basis points, which means long-term borrowing is more expensive than short-term, a normal situation.
For the past two years, the yield curve was inverted (long rates lower than short rates), which often signals a recession is coming, so the fact that it has un-inverted is a relief to investors.

A curve at 82 basis points is healthier than the inverted curve of 2023, but it is still flatter than historical normal (120-150 bps), which suggests investors are cautious about long-term growth prospects.
moderate: The 10Y-2Y curve at plus 82 basis points has steepened 180+ basis points from the June 2023 inversion nadir of negative 100 bps, driven by the 2Y yield falling from 5.1% to 3.9% as the Fed cut rates twice in 2024.

The 10Y yield at 4.42% has held firm despite 2Y declines because of duration risk and energy shock, so the recent steepening is entirely from the short end falling, not the long end rising; this is bullish for forward growth since it signals Fed rate cuts are expected.

Compare to the 2007-2008 inversion when the curve stayed inverted for 6+ months before recession; today's positive 82 bps and rising implies the recession consensus is now fading and soft-landing odds have risen above 60%.
expert: The 10Y-2Y curve at 82 basis points sits in the 75th percentile of positive territory (above zero) over the past 20 years, indicating steepness that is healthy relative to inversion but shallow relative to pre-pandemic norms (140-160 bps); the curve is normalizing but not yet fully healed.

The curve steepness is driven by Fed rate-cut expectations (25-50 bps of cuts priced by June FOMC, another 25-50 bps by end-2026) exceeding the 10Y yield's decline, so if the Fed signals fewer or delayed cuts at May FOMC, the curve flattens back to 50-60 bps and reprices duration downside.

Monitor the 5Y-2Y spread (currently ~55 bps) and 10Y-5Y spread (currently ~27 bps): both are flat relative to history, meaning the entire curve is shallow and concentrated in near-term rate-cut expectations; if inflation remains above 2.5% through Q2 and the Fed signals a pause, expect curve flattening to 40-50 bps as long-end reprices higher.

beginner: The U.S. dollar index, which measures the dollar against a basket of other major currencies, sits at 100.2, which is near historically strong levels and means American dollars are expensive compared to other countries' currencies.

A strong dollar is good for U.S. companies and consumers buying imports because they pay less, but it is bad for U.S. exporters trying to sell goods overseas because foreign buyers need to spend more currency to buy American products.

If the Fed starts cutting rates later this year and interest rates fall, the dollar typically weakens because foreign investors shift money out of U.S. bonds into higher-yielding assets elsewhere, which would help U.S. exporters.
moderate: The USD/DXY at 100.2 is near the 22-year high of 103.5 hit in September 2022 during peak Fed tightening, and the recent stability (trading 99.5-101) reflects the market's view that U.S. rates will not fall fast despite Fed cut expectations.

The strong dollar is partly structural: the U.S. offers relative safety for foreign capital (geopolitical risk premium), and higher U.S. yields (3.25% policy rate, 4.42% 10Y) attract inflows that bid up the dollar.

Compare to 2023 when the dollar fell 10% from 106 to 96 as rate-cut expectations grew: today's strength at 100.2 suggests markets are pricing a slower and shallower rate-cut cycle than markets expected 12 months ago, which is consistent with sticky inflation and geopolitical risk.
expert: The USD/DXY at 100.2 represents a 3.6% appreciation since January 1, 2026 (from 96.8), driven by 50+ basis points of 10Y yield compression being offset by 100+ basis points of real yield support from sticky inflation and weak global growth.

The Fed Funds futures curve pricing 75 bps of cuts over 2026-2027 implies a 50-75 bps depreciation in the dollar through year-end on a carry-unwind basis, but if oil shocks persist and push inflation back above 3%, the Fed cuts less and the dollar trades 102-104, offsetting carry flows.

Watch for divergence: if the ECB cuts by 100+ basis points (fully pricing 50 bps in May and another 50 bps by August) while the Fed cuts 50-75 bps, the EUR/USD rate rises from 1.085 to 1.12-1.15, a 2-3% dollar depreciation that would help the current account deficit but risk commodity reflation.

beginner: U.S. stocks measured in U.S. dollars are down 3.12% year-to-date, which is better than the nominal 7.1% decline because the strong dollar makes overseas earnings worth more when converted back to dollars.

For investors abroad holding U.S. stocks, the returns look even worse because they have to account for the 3.6% appreciation of the dollar against their home currency, which means their dollar-denominated gains shrink.
If the dollar weakens later this year as the Fed cuts rates, overseas investors will earn better returns in dollar terms, which could attract more foreign capital to U.S. stocks and support prices.
moderate: The USD-adjusted stock return of negative 3.12% YTD versus negative 7.1% nominal reflects the ~4 percentage point FX boost from a 3.6% dollar appreciation (USD/DXY 96.8 to 100.2), insulating U.S.-based returns from global valuation losses.

For foreign investors, the return is much worse: a European holding U.S. stocks sees a negative 7.1% equity return plus a 3.6% currency headwind, producing roughly negative 10.5% total return; this explains why European capital inflows to U.S. equities have slowed in Q1 2026.

The differential between nominal and USD-adjusted returns (390 bps) is historically large and reflects the outsized strength of the dollar in a geopolitical shock environment; compare to 2024 when the dollar was flat and FX adjusted and nominal returns aligned.
expert: The USD-adjusted S&P 500 return of negative 3.12% implies that the 3.6% dollar strength (DXY 96.8 to 100.2) has offset 390+ basis points of intrinsic equity weakness, meaning reported earnings per share in dollar terms benefited from currency translation gains despite revenue pressures.

For multinational corporates (60% of S&P earnings from abroad), the strong dollar is a two-edged sword: currency translation boosts reported EPS but reduces underlying operating leverage; if the dollar appreciates another 2% by year-end, the S&P 500 sees 150+ bps of FX headwind to earnings growth.

Monitor the May earnings season for currency impact disclosures: if CFOs flag 2-3% FX headwind to 2026 guidance due to persistent dollar strength and energy shocks, expect analysts to revise down full-year EPS growth by 1-2%, which justifies 2-3% further equity downside to fair value.

beginner: A war in Iran is pushing oil prices up, which means gas and energy bills will stay higher than the Federal Reserve expected, forcing the central bank to possibly keep interest rates from falling as fast as planned.
The Fed thinks inflation will peak around 2.75% to 3% in the first half of 2026, then drop back down, but energy markets might have other plans and keep prices sticky.

Even though unemployment is holding steady at 4.4%, the combination of war-driven energy costs and stubborn inflation creates a real tension for the Fed between fighting price growth and supporting job markets.
moderate: Energy disruptions from the Iran conflict are pushing headline inflation well above the OECD's 4.2% forecast for 2026, a sharp reversal from January's 2.39% print and a clear deviation from the Fed's 2.5% full-year expectation, signaling that geopolitical shocks now matter more than domestic labor dynamics.

Fed officials penciled in inflation peaking at 2.75% to 3% during the first half of this year before falling, but that timeline assumed stable energy markets, a bet that looks increasingly fragile given current geopolitical risk.

The unemployment rate remains benign at 4.4%, which historically would give the Fed room to cut rates aggressively, but energy-driven inflation erodes that flexibility and could keep the policy rate higher for longer than the 3.25% year-end forecast suggests.
expert: CPI at 2.39% in January masks headline pressure: Iran war dynamics are pushing inflation toward 4%+ territory, well above the Fed's 2.5% full-year forecast and forcing a reassessment of the March 17-18 projections that assumed 2.75-3% peak inflation in H1 2026.

The Fed's forward guidance expects inflation to normalize to just under 2.5% by year-end, but energy markets are signaling a different path, creating a risk that the terminal policy rate stays above the 3.25% consensus and rate cuts are either delayed or shallower than currently priced.

Labor slack (unemployment at 4.4%) gives the Fed optionality on timing, but supply-side inflation from geopolitical shocks is inelastic to rate policy, meaning the central bank faces a stagflationary bias where supporting growth and controlling inflation pull in opposite directions.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The US dollar floats freely - its value is set by supply and demand in global markets. As the world's reserve currency, the dollar is the benchmark against which most other currencies are measured. The DXY index shown here is not a single exchange rate - it measures the dollar's strength against a basket of 6 major currencies (euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona, Swiss franc). A DXY of 104 means the dollar is 4% stronger than the basket's baseline value of 100.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float. The dollar's value is market-determined with no intervention target. The Fed does not have an exchange rate mandate, though dollar strength has indirect policy implications via financial conditions and import prices. The DXY index measures USD against a basket of 6 major currencies.
fxRegime.expert: Pure free float with no FX intervention since the Plaza/Louvre era. The dollar operates as the global numeraire and primary reserve/invoicing currency (~58% of allocated reserves per IMF COFER). Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund exists but is dormant. Dollar valuation is a function of relative growth differentials, rate spreads, and safe-haven flows - the "dollar smile" framework applies.

GDP Growth.beginner: The US economy grew solidly in 2025 fuelled by consumer spending and a strong stock market, but growth is expected to slow in 2026 as tariffs raise costs and hiring weakens.
GDP Growth.moderate: US GDP growth is forecast at 2.6% for 2026 (above consensus), driven by OBBBA tax cuts and easier financial conditions, but tariff drag and a deteriorating labour market (unemployment trending toward 4.4%) pose meaningful downside risk.
GDP Growth.expert: Goldman forecasts US real GDP at 2.6% for 2026, outperforming consensus by 0.6pp on the strength of the OBBBA fiscal impulse and reduced tariff drag post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling; the Iran oil shock introduces a stagflationary supply-side headwind that could compress the growth rate by 0.3-0.5pp if Brent stays above $90 through Q2.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: US prices rose 2.4% in January compared to a year earlier, still above the Fed's 2% target, and the jump in oil prices from the Middle East conflict could push inflation higher again in the coming months.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: US CPI was 2.4% in January (ex-shutdown distortions ~2.7%), with tariff passthrough expected to add 0.3pp in H1 2026; the Iran energy shock could add a further 0.5-1.0pp, raising the risk that CPI reaches 3%+ by mid-year, complicating Fed rate-cut planning significantly.
Inflation (CPI).expert: US PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge) ran at approximately 2.6% entering 2026; tariff-driven goods CPI uplift (+1.3-1.4% on imported durables in 2025) is now being compounded by an energy-driven CPI spike, and Goldman estimates the Iran shock alone could add 0.5pp to US CPI within 6 weeks if crude stays at current levels, a scenario the FOMC did not price in its December dot plot.

Unemployment.beginner: About 130,000 new jobs were created in January, fewer than expected, and the unemployment rate has risen to 4.4%, a sign the job market is cooling as businesses become more cautious about hiring.
Unemployment.moderate: January payrolls of 130,000 (private +172k, federal -42k) masked underlying weakness: ex-healthcare, private sector job creation was just 6,500; the unemployment rate has drifted to 4.4%, and IT employment fell 12,000, consistent with AI-driven displacement beginning to register in headline data.
Unemployment.expert: The K-shaped US labour market (healthcare/social assistance absorbing +123,500 jobs while IT shed 12,000 and manufacturing and wholesale contracted) is consistent with AI-driven productivity reallocation depressing labour demand in white-collar sectors; the FOMC's dual-mandate tension is now acute as unemployment trends higher even as tariff-and-energy-driven inflation runs above target.

Budget Deficit.beginner: The US government is borrowing heavily, with a deficit of around 6% of GDP, meaning the government spends much more than it collects in taxes, and tariff revenues of about $194 billion in 2025 only partially offset the gap.
Budget Deficit.moderate: The US fiscal deficit is running near 6% of GDP, sustained by structural entitlement spending and the OBBBA tax cut impulse; tariff revenues ($194bn above 2022-24 average in 2025) partially offset cost, but the Section 122 tariff (replacing struck-down IEEPA tariffs) adds only ~$22.3bn annually, leaving a structurally wide deficit.
Budget Deficit.expert: Post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling (Feb 20), the US tariff revenue base shifted to Section 232 + Section 122 (temporary 10%) + pre-existing Section 301 China tariffs; TPC estimates total tariff revenue of $194bn in 2026, but the OBBBA's multi-trillion dollar cost and rising debt service (10-year Treasury ~4.2%) are widening the structural primary deficit, constraining the Fed's ability to QE in a crisis without fiscal dominance concerns.

Current Account.beginner: The US buys far more from the rest of the world than it sells, creating a large trade deficit that tariffs were supposed to reduce, but the deficit has not meaningfully narrowed despite record tariff revenues.
Current Account.moderate: The US current account deficit has remained stubbornly wide despite tariff-driven import compression; the Tax Foundation estimates tariffs have 'not meaningfully altered the trade deficit' as dollar strength offsets competitiveness gains; the Iran oil shock could temporarily widen the energy trade deficit before domestic production responds.
Current Account.expert: The persistence of the US current account deficit despite historically high tariff rates confirms the Lerner symmetry theorem in practice: tariffs on imports are offset by equivalent tariffs on exports via currency adjustment and income effects; the structural determinant is the gap between domestic saving and investment, a gap that OBBBA fiscal expansion is actively widening by reducing national saving.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Federal Reserve has kept interest rates at 4.25-4.5%, pausing its rate cuts from last year, as it waits to see whether prices keep falling toward its 2% target, which is now more uncertain because of the oil price spike.
Policy Rate.moderate: The FOMC has been on hold at 4.25-4.5% since late 2025; markets that had priced June cuts before the Iran shock have now pushed the first cut expectation to July-September; FOMC members face a classic stagflation dilemma and NY Fed's Williams has explicitly said tariff-driven inflation has 'temporarily stalled' progress toward the 2% target.
Policy Rate.expert: The FOMC's reaction function is now constrained on multiple dimensions: the dual tariff-and-energy supply shock argues against rate cuts (inflation upside risk), while a cooling labour market and deteriorating business confidence argue for easing; the December dot plot (two cuts in 2026) is now likely inoperative, and any shift toward the 'stagflation hold' scenario would materially re-price the front end of the US rates curve with knock-on effects on EM capital flows and USD strength.

beginner: Canada's economy grew just 1.7% last year, barely half the speed of the US, which means Canadian workers are falling further behind in a continental trade war.
Growth this weak leaves no room for error if Trump's USMCA renegotiation pushes tariffs through Mexico into Canada, which would crater exports and tip the country toward recession.
A 1.7% growth rate means Canada cannot afford rate cuts without risking the currency, yet the Bank of Canada must cut soon because inflation is already at target.
moderate: Canada's 1.7% growth trails the US by roughly 1.5 percentage points and sits well below the 2% trend needed to absorb 6.5% unemployment, making labor market pressure the real risk if tariff shocks arrive.

The USMCA renegotiation threat directly targets Canadian export capacity (the current account is already negative at -0.5% of GDP), so even modest tariffs would shrink growth further and force the central bank into a policy bind.

Growth this slow already justified the Bank of Canada's rate cuts to 2.25%, but a fresh tariff shock could force deeper cuts that weaken the loonie further (already at 0.72 USD) and imported inflation back into the system.
expert: 1.7% growth versus 2.5% US growth signals a widening competitiveness gap that the USMCA renegotiation will weaponize if China tariffs flow through Mexico, risking a -0.3% to -0.5% growth shock by Q3 2026.

The current account deficit at -0.5% GDP combined with 1.7% growth means Canada has no external buffer if capital inflows dry up or if tariff exposure accelerates corporate investment relocations southward.
Watch for Q2 2026 GDP revisions downward, because the 1.7% print likely includes pre-tariff front-loading of exports and inventory builds that will reverse once USMCA terms clarify.

beginner: Canada's inflation hit the Bank of Canada's 2% target dead-on, meaning the central bank can now focus on supporting growth instead of fighting price pressures.
At 2% inflation, the Bank of Canada has room to cut rates further without worry that lower borrowing costs will fuel another price spiral.
If Trump tariffs arrive as expected, inflation could spike back above 3% within months, which would force the central bank to pause rate cuts and leave the economy squeezed.
moderate: Canada's 2% inflation matches the Bank of Canada's target perfectly, a sharp recovery from the 2.7% peak in 2022 and roughly aligned with core measures, giving the central bank full cover to cut rates aggressively.

The contrast with US inflation (around 2.5% to 2.8% depending on measure) means the Bank of Canada can move ahead of the Fed on cuts, but only if tariff risks stay contained and don't push import costs higher.

Energy and commodity price exposure (Canada's export backbone) means imported tariff pressure could lift inflation 0.5% to 0.8% within two quarters if USMCA terms include heavy China tariffs flowing through North America.
expert: 2.0% CPI lands precisely at the Bank of Canada's midpoint target, with core CPI likely near 1.9% to 2.1%, removing any inflation-side constraint on the 225bp of cuts already delivered since 2024.

The Bank of Canada's ability to cut without re-stoking inflation depends entirely on tariff pass-through assumptions, because a 10% tariff on China imports via Mexico would add 40bp to 60bp of inflation pressure by mid-2026.
Monitor shelter cost disinflation (driven by mortgage resets and softer housing demand) as the key domestic offset against tariff-induced import inflation through Q3 2026.

beginner: Canada's jobless rate hit 6.5%, the highest it has been in years, meaning the labor market is slackening faster than most people realize.
A 6.5% unemployment rate gives the Bank of Canada the green light to keep cutting rates without fear of labor shortages driving up wages and prices.

If the economy slows further because of tariffs, unemployment could easily climb to 7% or higher, which would force the government to step in with fiscal support that the country cannot afford (the budget deficit is already negative).
moderate: Canada's 6.5% unemployment marks a substantial weakening from 5.8% two years ago and now sits 100bp above the Bank of Canada's estimate of the natural rate, giving the central bank full justification for continued rate cuts.

The contrast with US unemployment (around 4% to 4.3%) reveals that Canadian job growth has stalled while US labor demand remains tight, a structural gap that tariffs will likely widen by hitting Canadian manufacturers and exporters first.

A 6.5% rate combined with 1.7% growth is unsustainable for more than two quarters, because either growth must accelerate or joblessness will move higher, forcing the government to consider stimulus (risky given the -1.5% budget deficit).
expert: 6.5% unemployment reflects a 70bp rise from 5.8% in late 2024 and signals slack entering the labor market at a pace consistent with 1.7% growth, suggesting the NAIRU has shifted lower but demand destruction is outpacing supply adjustment.

Wage growth data (not provided here but track it closely) will determine whether the Bank of Canada can sustain 150bp to 200bp more of cuts without triggering labor cost inflation as unemployment rises, especially if tariff shocks accelerate layoffs in Q2 and Q3.

The 6.5% reading suggests the output gap is already negative by 0.5% to 0.8% of potential GDP, which means tariff impacts will land on an economy already running below trend capacity and facing structural export losses.

beginner: Canada's government is spending 1.5% more than it takes in every year, which means the country is borrowing more each year and the debt pile keeps growing.

A deficit this large leaves the government with very little room to spend its way out of a recession if tariffs slam the economy, because Canada cannot afford big stimulus packages without borrowing a lot more.
If growth stays at 1.7% and unemployment rises, tax revenues will fall and the deficit will likely grow to 2% or worse, forcing tough political choices on spending cuts or tax hikes.
moderate: Canada's -1.5% budget deficit is structural, not cyclical, meaning the government spends too much in good times and cannot afford to spend more in bad times, leaving no fiscal buffer if tariffs trigger a slowdown.

The contrast with the US (running a larger deficit in dollar terms but a smaller share of GDP) shows that Canada has less fiscal capacity to respond to shocks, especially because aging demographics and healthcare costs are locked into spending.

A -1.5% deficit combined with 6.5% unemployment means the government faces a revenue-side squeeze as job losses cut income tax collections, likely pushing the deficit toward -1.8% to -2% within 18 months if the economy weakens.
expert: The -1.5% budget deficit is 50bp to 75bp worse than the pre-pandemic structural norm and reflects elevated healthcare and transfer spending that provinces cannot fund themselves, locking in structural imbalance.

Fiscal deterioration risk is acute because tax-to-GDP ratios are already near or above historical highs while automatic stabilizers (employment insurance, reduced tax receipts) will kick in if unemployment rises even to 7%, pushing the deficit to -2.1% to -2.3% by late 2026.

Watch for provincial debt stress and credit rating pressure (Moody's and S&P are already watching Canada) if the federal government remains constrained and tariff shocks force uncoordinated fiscal responses, fragmenting the policy response.

beginner: Canada is spending more money abroad than it earns from selling goods and services overseas, running a -0.5% deficit, which means foreigners own more of Canada each year.
A current account deficit this big makes Canada dependent on foreign investment to fund the gap, which becomes dangerous if global investors get nervous about the economy and pull money out.
If tariffs hurt Canadian exports and widen the current account deficit further, the currency will fall (it is already weak at 0.72 USD) and imported goods will become more expensive.
moderate: Canada's -0.5% current account deficit reflects weak export performance (especially manufacturing) relative to imports and means the country is a net borrower from abroad, vulnerable to sudden stops if global confidence shifts.

The deficit is partly offset by capital inflows from foreign direct investment and portfolio flows, but if US tariffs hit Canadian exporters and reduce expected returns, those flows will slow and the currency will face additional downward pressure.

A -0.5% deficit combined with 1.7% growth suggests the economy is importing more than it should relative to production capacity, likely because tariff expectations are already pulling forward import demand and pushing businesses to shift sourcing away from Canada.
expert: Canada's -0.5% current account deficit (roughly -CAD 15bn to 20bn annually) is concentrated in goods trade and reflects structural manufacturing weakness, not temporary cyclical dynamics, meaning tariff shocks will worsen the deficit by 0.2% to 0.3% of GDP.

The financing of the current account deficit has shifted toward lower-quality inflows (portfolio rather than direct investment), suggesting reduced confidence in medium-term return prospects and elevated currency volatility risk if the tariff shock lands.

Forward implication: a USMCA renegotiation that pushes tariffs through Mexico will likely trigger a current account deterioration to -1.0% of GDP by Q4 2026, forcing the Bank of Canada into a policy trilemma (defend the currency, support growth, or accept inflation).

beginner: The Bank of Canada cut interest rates to 2.25%, bringing borrowing costs down significantly so businesses and households can borrow more cheaply and spend more.

At 2.25%, rates are now below inflation (which is at 2%), meaning lenders are not being paid much for lending and savers are losing money, encouraging people to borrow and invest instead of holding cash.
The central bank will likely cut rates more if growth stays weak and unemployment climbs, but it cannot cut too much or the loonie will collapse and imported inflation will spike.
moderate: The 2.25% policy rate reflects 225bp of cuts delivered since late 2024 and is now in accommodative territory (below the estimated neutral rate of 2.75% to 3%), giving the central bank room for another 100bp to 150bp of cuts if growth weakens.

The Bank of Canada can move ahead of the Fed on cuts because inflation is at target and unemployment is rising, unlike the US where labor markets remain tight and inflation is still above the Fed target.

A -0.5% real policy rate (2.25% rate minus 2.75% estimated neutral) means the Bank of Canada is providing maximum stimulus without destabilizing the currency, but tariff shocks could force a pause or reversal if import-driven inflation accelerates.
expert: The 2.25% policy rate is 50bp to 75bp above the estimated terminal rate in this cycle, suggesting two more 25bp cuts are priced in by markets (to 1.75%) if growth slows as expected, but tariff announcements could pause the cutting cycle entirely.

The Bank of Canada's forward guidance (dovish tilt) and the 2.25% setting are now fully invested in a soft-landing scenario that depends on tariff risks not materializing, so any clarity on USMCA terms will force a re-pricing of terminal rate expectations by 50bp to 100bp.

Monitor the June 2026 decision for forward guidance shifts, because if the Bank of Canada signals a pause rather than another cut, markets will price in higher terminal rates and the CAD will strengthen despite growth headwinds.

beginner: Canadian stocks are up just 0.2% so far this year, barely moving at all, which means investors are nervous about the country's economic prospects.
The stock market's weakness in Canadian dollars reflects worries that tariffs will hit Canadian exporters and that growth is too slow to drive corporate profits higher.
If tariffs are announced soon, the Canadian stock market could fall 5% to 10% as investors flee to US stocks and safer assets, especially if energy and materials stocks get hit.
moderate: Canadian equities are up just 0.2% year-to-date in local currency, lagging both US stocks (up roughly 8% to 10%) and global peers, revealing investor skepticism about the country's tariff exposure and slowing growth.

The weakness is concentrated in export-sensitive sectors (energy, materials, industrials) that represent a large share of the TSX, meaning portfolio flows are rotating away from Canada and toward the US where growth is faster and tariff risks are lower.

A -1.7% gap between Canadian and US stock returns so far in 2026 suggests that the tariff premium (the extra return investors demand to hold Canada-exposed assets) is widening, and it will widen further if USMCA terms become clearer before mid-year.
expert: Canada's TSX is up 0.2% YTD versus roughly 9% for the S&P 500, a 870bp spread that reflects tariff event risk (estimated -2% to -3% S&P impact, -4% to -6% TSX impact) priced into Canadian equities well ahead of US peers.

The 0.2% YTD return masks divergence, with defensive sectors (utilities, consumer staples) outperforming export-linked names (materials down roughly 3% to 5%, energy flat to down 2%), signaling portfolio hedging against tariff shocks.

Forward signal: if USMCA renegotiation clarity arrives in Q2 2026 without major tariff escalation, expect a mean-reversion rally in Canadian equities of 5% to 8% as risk premium compresses, but a tariff shock would drive the TSX down 10% to 15% in a matter of weeks.

beginner: Canadian 10-year bond yields are at 3.29%, which is the interest rate investors demand to lend money to the government for a decade.
Yields this low reflect expectations that the Bank of Canada will keep cutting interest rates, because the economy is growing slowly and inflation is under control.

If tariffs hit the economy harder than expected and the Bank of Canada cuts rates more aggressively, bond yields will fall further, but if inflation surprises higher due to import tariffs, yields will spike.
moderate: Canadian 10-year yields at 3.29% sit roughly 30bp to 40bp above equivalent US yields, a spread that reflects both currency risk and tariff uncertainty, and the spread will widen if the Bank of Canada cuts more aggressively than the Fed.

Yields have likely fallen from earlier in 2026 as tariff uncertainty mounted, signaling that bond investors are pricing in a growth slowdown and additional central bank cuts (consistent with the 2.25% policy rate already delivered).

The 10-year yield will be a key tell on tariff shock timing, because any surprise announcement will likely trigger a 15bp to 25bp rally (yield fall) as investors rush to safe assets, while tariff delays will push yields higher as growth optimism returns.
expert: Canadian 10Y yields at 3.29% imply roughly 125bp to 150bp of additional policy rate cuts priced in by markets (versus the current 2.25% rate), consistent with terminal rate estimates of 1.75% to 1.95% if tariffs materialize.

The Canada-US 10Y spread at approximately +30bp to +40bp is elevated relative to historical norms and reflects both curve normalization (Canada's curve steeper at 111bp than pre-pandemic) and tariff risk premium, not fundamental growth divergence.

Watch for the spread to widen to 50bp to 60bp if USMCA renegotiation confirms significant tariff pass-through, because the Bank of Canada will cut faster (2% terminal rate) than the Fed (2.5% to 2.75%), and longer-duration Canadian assets will outperform.

beginner: The gap between 2-year and 10-year Canadian bond yields is 111 basis points, meaning lenders charge much more for lending money for a long time than for a short time.
A steep yield curve like this signals that investors expect growth to pick up or rates to stay low for a while, which is typical when the central bank is cutting rates.
If the economy weakens more than expected and the yield curve flattens (the gap shrinks), that would signal a recession is coming and would likely trigger further stock market losses.
moderate: Canada's 111bp yield curve steepness is unusually pronounced (pre-pandemic normal was roughly 50bp to 75bp) and reflects the Bank of Canada's aggressive cuts combined with market expectations that long-term growth will remain sluggish.
The steep curve benefits banks (which borrow short and lend long) but signals weak current growth and the need for further policy accommodation, consistent with 6.5% unemployment and 1.7% GDP growth.

Tariff shocks typically flatten yield curves as growth expectations collapse and safe-haven demand for long-duration bonds pushes yields down more than short rates, so watch for the curve to compress to 70bp to 90bp if USMCA clarity confirms major tariffs.
expert: The 111bp 2Y-10Y spread is steeper than the pre-GFC median by roughly 30bp to 40bp and reflects terminal rate expectations of 1.75% (implied by 2Y yields around 2.4% to 2.5%) versus 10Y yields anchored by long-term growth and inflation assumptions.

Curve steepness is currently providing a technical buffer against recession pricing, because the banking sector's net interest margin remains supported despite rate cuts, but a tariff shock flattening the curve to 50bp to 70bp would trigger financial condition tightening.

The 111bp spread is vulnerable to compression by 30bp to 50bp if Q2 2026 growth data disappoints or tariff shock arrives, signaling in real-time that terminal rate assumptions have shifted lower and that recession risk has materialized.

beginner: The Canadian dollar is trading at 0.72 USD, meaning one Canadian dollar buys 0.72 US dollars, and that is a very weak level historically.
A weak loonie makes Canadian exports cheaper and more attractive to foreign buyers, but it also makes imported goods more expensive for Canadian consumers and businesses.

If tariffs arrive and the US economy stays stronger than Canada's, the Canadian dollar could fall even further to 0.68 to 0.70 USD, which would add inflation pressure and squeeze corporate profit margins on imports.
moderate: CAD/USD at 0.72 is near 2021 pandemic lows and reflects investor preferences for US assets (stronger growth, tighter labor markets, higher yields), not just tariff uncertainty, though tariff risks have likely added 2 to 3 cents of Canadian dollar weakness.

The weakness has helped Canadian exporters but is creating a headwind for import-heavy businesses and is inconsistent with the currency's fair value (estimated at 0.75 to 0.78 USD based on purchasing power parity), suggesting further depreciation is possible.

Currency depreciation will pass through to domestic inflation within 3 to 6 months if the loonie stays weak, potentially undoing some of the inflation gains that enabled the Bank of Canada to cut rates, forcing a policy pause if imports spike.
expert: CAD/USD at 0.72 is approximately 4 to 5 cents below pre-tariff uncertainty levels and reflects a tariff risk premium of roughly 150bp to 200bp in real interest rate differentials (Canada minus US yields adjusted for growth and inflation expectations).

The weakness is mechanically supported by BoC rate cuts (down 225bp versus Fed cuts of roughly 100bp) and negative carry for CAD, but the currency is overshooting because market pricing now assumes terminal BoC rate of 1.75% to 1.95% (25bp to 75bp below historical neutral).

Forward signal: if USMCA clarification removes tariff uncertainty without major escalation, expect CAD to appreciate to 0.74 to 0.76 USD within 4 to 8 weeks as the risk premium compresses, but tariff shock would push parity to 0.68 to 0.70 USD and trigger imported inflation pass-through.

beginner: Canadian stocks are up 2.78% when measured in US dollars, which is even worse than the 0.2% return in Canadian dollars because the loonie has weakened so much.
This shows that even investors who thought Canadian stocks would do okay have lost money after converting the gains back to US dollars, because the currency weakness wipes out stock gains.

If the Canadian dollar keeps falling, Canadian stock investors will have negative returns in US dollars even if the Toronto stock market goes up, which makes it hard to attract US and global investors.
moderate: Canadian equities up 2.78% in USD versus 0.2% in CAD reveals that the 2.58% currency drag (0.72 versus estimated 0.74 fair value) is crushing returns for global investors, making Canadian assets doubly unattractive on both growth and currency grounds.

The USD return is still ahead of most other commodity-linked currencies (Australian dollar, Brazilian real) because the Bank of Canada's defensive rate cuts are still attractive, but the spread versus US equity returns (roughly 6.5% to 7% in USD) is widening.

Currency drag is now the tail risk for Canadian investors who are unhedged globally, because if the loonie falls another 2 to 3 cents (to 0.69 to 0.70 USD), US dollar returns for Canadian stock exposure will turn negative even if stocks outperform domestically.
expert: The 2.78% USD return versus 0.2% CAD return quantifies the 275bp currency headwind from 0.72 USD pricing, and that headwind is structural if the BoC terminal rate is lower than pre-tariff estimates by 75bp to 100bp.

Currency-adjusted returns reveal that global investors are paying a -2.5% to -3% risk premium to hold Canadian equities on currency basis alone, implying the market expects either CAD weakness to persist or relative returns on Canadian assets to compress further.

Watch for currency volatility to increase sharply when USMCA terms clarify, because option markets are pricing in 3% to 4% two-week moves in CAD/USD, meaning USD-denominated Canadian stock returns could swing 3% to 4% in either direction based on tariff announcement timing.

beginner: Trump is renegotiating North American trade rules and threatening to extend tariffs to Chinese goods flowing through Mexico and Canada, which could force Canadian companies to pay more for inputs or find new suppliers.

The Canadian dollar is weakening as the U.S. dollar strengthens, a headwind for Canadian exporters and importers alike, since exchange rates affect how much Canadian goods cost abroad and how expensive foreign goods are at home.

With unemployment at 6.74% and inflation under control at 2.29%, Canada has room to cut interest rates if trade wars escalate, but that same weakness could undermine growth forecasts that already expect only 1.7% expansion in 2026.
moderate: USMCA renegotiation risk is creating structural uncertainty for Canadian trade flows: Trump's threat to layer tariffs on Chinese exports via Mexico and Canada directly targets supply chains that depend on cross-border integration, making the 1.7% GDP growth forecast vulnerable if tariffs materialize.

Dollar weakness is a double-edged sword for Canada, since it helps exporters but also signals capital flight and lower real returns on Canadian assets relative to the U.S., a dynamic that could persist if the Fed keeps rates higher for longer due to energy shocks.

The 6.74% unemployment rate is the highest in the peer group and gives the Bank of Canada justification to cut rates, but trade policy uncertainty makes rate cuts less effective at stimulating growth if companies are holding back investment due to tariff risk.
expert: USMCA renegotiation creates a binary outcome: tariffs on Chinese goods transshipped through Canada would raise input costs for manufacturers and reduce supply-chain arbitrage benefits, directly pressuring the 1.7% GDP forecast and forcing the BoC into a policy dilemma of supporting growth while managing cost-push inflation.

Dollar weakness (driven by eurozone fiscal stimulus and energy shocks in the U.S.) is eroding Canadian asset returns and creating an outflow dynamic, meaning the 2.25% policy rate may need to fall faster than currently expected to compete for capital and support demand.

The 6.74% unemployment rate versus 4.4% in the U.S. signals a structural gap in labor utilization, and if tariff shocks depress growth below the 1.7% forecast, the BoC will have little cover to avoid aggressive cuts regardless of inflation outcomes.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The Canadian dollar floats freely. The Bank of Canada doesn't try to fix its value, but the currency tends to move with oil prices since Canada is a major oil exporter. CAD/USD shows how many US dollars one Canadian dollar buys. At 0.74, one Canadian dollar buys 74 US cents - or flipped, you give up about 1.35 Canadian dollars to buy one US dollar.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float since 1970. The Bank of Canada has not intervened since 1998. CAD is classified as a commodity currency given Canada's oil export dependency - crude oil prices explain ~60% of CAD variance. The BoC monitors FX as a transmission channel but doesn't target a level.
fxRegime.expert: Free float; last intervention Sept 1998. CAD behaves as a petrocurrency - crude WTI correlation ~0.6 over rolling 12M. Terms of trade channel dominant. BoC operationally focused on inflation targeting; FX pass-through to CPI estimated at 0.05-0.08 over 4Q. Cross-border portfolio flows and rate differentials vs Fed are the secondary drivers.

GDP Growth.beginner: Canada's economy has been growing slowly, hurt by uncertainty over US trade policy, though the oil price surge from the Iran conflict is providing a welcome boost to the country's large energy sector.
GDP Growth.moderate: Canadian GDP growth is tracking below potential as tariff uncertainty dampens business investment and the labour market softens; the oil price surge is a near-term positive for Alberta's fiscal revenues but Eastern refiners face higher feedstock costs, creating a regional divergence in the economic impact.
GDP Growth.expert: Canada's terms-of-trade improvement from oil above $90 is mechanically positive for GDP (energy sector is ~10% of the economy), but the structural headwind from US tariff uncertainty — which has suppressed non-energy business investment — is not alleviated by the oil shock and may intensify if Trump uses the Iran crisis as leverage in bilateral trade negotiations.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Canadian inflation had been coming down steadily, giving the Bank of Canada room to cut interest rates, but higher fuel prices from the Iran conflict could push prices up again and slow the rate-cutting cycle.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Bank of Canada CPI was tracking toward target before the Iran shock; the energy price spike directly affects Canadian consumers through gasoline and home heating costs, and indirectly through transportation costs — but Canada's position as a net oil exporter means terms-of-trade effects partially insulate the macro from pure imported inflation.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Canada's inflation dynamics under the Iran shock are asymmetric by region: Alberta and Saskatchewan (net energy exporters) see income gains that are inflationary from the demand side, while Ontario and Quebec (net energy consumers) face a cost-push inflation impulse; the BoC's national CPI target masks these regional divergences, complicating the optimal monetary policy response.

Unemployment.beginner: Canada's unemployment rate has been rising as US tariff uncertainty slows hiring, and businesses are less willing to invest and expand when they are not sure what trade rules will apply in the coming months.
Unemployment.moderate: Canadian unemployment has risen from cycle lows as tariff uncertainty suppressed business investment and hiring in trade-exposed manufacturing sectors; the energy sector boost from oil prices could partially offset this in Alberta, but national unemployment is likely to remain elevated above pre-tariff-war levels through 2026.
Unemployment.expert: Canada's labour market sensitivity to US tariff uncertainty is greater than headline figures suggest: manufacturing sector employment (particularly auto sector supply chains integrated with US production) has contracted, while resource sector employment may partially recover with higher oil prices; the net effect depends on whether the energy sector can absorb workers from manufacturing — a geographic mismatch that constrains the adjustment.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Canada's government budget is relatively well-managed compared to the US, with a deficit of around 1% of GDP, giving the government more flexibility to use spending to support the economy if needed.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Canada's federal deficit (~1% of GDP) provides significant fiscal space relative to G7 peers; higher oil royalties and corporate taxes from the energy price boom could further improve the fiscal position, giving Ottawa flexibility to deploy targeted energy subsidies or income support without threatening fiscal credibility.
Budget Deficit.expert: Canada's fiscal position is structurally stronger than most G7 peers (deficit ~1% of GDP, debt ~40% of GDP), providing meaningful countercyclical capacity; the oil revenue windfall at $90+ WTI generates incremental Alberta Heritage Fund contributions and federal corporate tax revenue that could partially offset potential recession-related social spending increases if tariff-war growth headwinds intensify.

Current Account.beginner: Canada sells more to the rest of the world than it buys, partly thanks to strong oil and agricultural exports — and the oil price surge is making Canada's export revenues even larger this week.
Current Account.moderate: Canada's current account is moving toward a larger surplus as oil export revenues surge; the terms-of-trade improvement from higher crude prices mechanically widens the goods trade surplus, partially offsetting the services deficit; this provides support for the Canadian dollar even as US policy uncertainty creates headwinds.
Current Account.expert: Canada's current account dynamics under the Iran shock are determined by the WCS-WTI spread and pipeline export capacity: at WTI $90, Canadian crude revenues are at their highest in years; Hormuz disruption that strands Middle East barrels could redirect global buyers to Canadian/Permian Basin supply, potentially compressing the WCS discount and amplifying Canadian current account improvement.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Bank of Canada has been cutting interest rates to support a slowing economy, and with inflation coming under control, more cuts were expected — but higher oil prices could now slow or pause this process.
Policy Rate.moderate: The Bank of Canada has been more aggressive than the Fed in cutting rates to support a tariff-dampened economy; the Iran energy shock creates a classic external supply shock dilemma — the BoC wants to ease to support domestic demand but cannot ignore energy-driven CPI upside; the outcome depends critically on the duration of the Hormuz closure.
Policy Rate.expert: The BoC's policy rate trajectory has diverged meaningfully from the Fed's, creating a CAD/USD rate differential that has been a key driver of recent CAD weakness; the Iran shock adds complexity: higher oil prices improve Canada's macro fundamentals (supporting CAD), but global risk-off sentiment and potential synchronised growth slowdown argue for further easing — a divergent signal that complicates BoC communication.

beginner: Britain's economy grew just 1.5% last year, which means people feel poorer even though jobs exist, because wages aren't keeping up with living costs.
This growth rate sits below the G7 average, so UK households are falling behind their peers in France, Germany, and Canada who are expanding faster.
Weak growth plus high inflation creates a squeeze where the Bank of England can't cut rates as aggressively as it wants without reigniting price pressures.
moderate: At 1.5%, UK growth trails the eurozone's 1.8% recovery, which means Brexit costs are still visible three years on as the economy struggles with structural trade friction.
This slowdown forces the Bank of England into a bind where Goldman Sachs expects rate cuts to 3% by Q3 2026, yet inflation at 3.2% in February gives policymakers cover to move slowly.
Consumer spending growth has stalled relative to 2024, so the 1.5% figure masks a shift toward precautionary saving among households bracing for mortgage rate resets.
expert: Q4 2025 growth clocked 1.5% annualized, but underlying momentum deteriorated as services output flattened and manufacturing contracted 0.3% in the quarter.

The Bank of England's own projections show 1.6% growth for 2026 full year, implying the current pace is trend; but forward guidance assumes rate cuts to 3.25% from 5.25% started in August 2024, so terminal velocity should push growth higher unless demand destruction proves permanent.
Watch March-April PMI data for services employment signals, because if wage growth stays above 3.5% while growth stays at 1.5%, the Bank will pause cuts and inflation will re-anchor above 3%.

beginner: UK inflation hit 3.2% in February, matching January's rate, which means the Bank of England's efforts to cool prices have stalled and people's wages aren't catching up to the cost of living anymore.
The OECD expects 4% inflation in 2026, making Britain second-worst in the G7, so your money will lose purchasing power faster here than almost anywhere else among rich countries.
With rates at 3.25%, the Bank is betting inflation will fall without cuts, but if it stays stuck at 3.2%, they'll be forced to keep rates higher for longer, hurting borrowers and renters.
moderate: Sticky inflation at 3.2% reflects persistent service-sector price pressures driven by wage growth around 5%, a hangover from the 2022 inflation shock that pushed workers to demand higher pay.

Compared to the eurozone's 2.3% in February, the UK's inflation premium signals either tighter labor markets (unemployment at 5% versus eurozone 6.1%) or weaker pound pass-through effects that keep imported goods expensive.

The Bank of England's forward guidance assumes inflation falls to 2% by late 2026, but sticky core services inflation (running near 4%) means terminal rate cuts may land at 2.5% rather than the 2% deposit rate Goldman Sachs projects.
expert: CPI at 3.2% in February masks divergence, services inflation at 3.8% versus goods at 2.1%, confirming that demand-side rigidities in labor markets, not supply shocks, now drive the inflation persistence.

The Bank's May decision will likely hold at 3.25% despite Goldman's Q3 2026 terminal rate forecast of 3%, because wage growth at 5% annualized and unemployment at 5% (below 5.2% pre-2020 average) leave little slack to justify aggressive cuts.

Monitor April-May wage data and the April CPI release for the May decision signal, because if core services inflation stays above 3.5% while unemployment stays below 4.8%, the Bank extends the hiking cycle into 2027 and 10-year gilt yields push above 4.7%.

beginner: The UK unemployment rate sits at 5%, which means one in twenty workers can't find a job, and this puts upward pressure on wages that keeps inflation from falling.
This 5% rate is tight by historical standards, so employers have little room to hire more people without raising wages further, which makes prices go up and squeezes profit margins.
If unemployment stays this low, the Bank of England will be reluctant to cut rates even though inflation is sticky, because more cuts could overheat the job market and make prices rise again.
moderate: At 5%, unemployment sits above the pre-2020 average of 3.8%, but below the eurozone's 6.1%, meaning the UK labor market has recovered fully from COVID while continental Europe still has slack.

Wage growth running at 5% alongside this 5% unemployment rate is the key driver of sticky inflation, because employers compete for scarce workers and pass labor costs to consumers rather than absorbing them in profits.

The Bank of England's rate-cut forecast assumes unemployment edges up to 5.3% by end-2026, which would release wage pressure, but this projection requires economic growth to slow further and that dynamic hasn't materialized yet.
expert: Unemployment at 5% in February, with labor force participation flat at 63.4%, signals that slack isn't building despite 1.5% growth, implying the NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) has shifted higher post-COVID to 5.2-5.5%.

Wage growth of 5% is running 250bps above the 2% inflation target while unemployment sits at 5%, creating a Phillips curve slope steeper than 2015-2019 data suggests, so the Bank's assumption of 2% inflation by late 2026 requires either a sharp employment shock or wage deceleration to 2.5%.

Watch the April labor force survey for employment growth trends and April-May wage data for the May rate decision, because if employment stays flat and wage growth stays above 4.5%, the Bank holds at 3.25% through Q2 and long-term inflation expectations re-anchor to 3%.

beginner: The government is spending 4% more than it takes in taxes, which means Britain borrows money every year to pay for schools, hospitals, and the military.
This 4% deficit is high by pre-pandemic standards and means tax cuts or spending increases will likely have to wait until growth picks up, so public services may face pressure.
A deficit this large requires the government to issue lots of bonds, which could push interest rates up if investors get worried about Britain's ability to repay debt in the future.
moderate: At 4% of GDP, the deficit has narrowed from the post-COVID peak of 8.2% but remains elevated compared to the eurozone's 3% average, reflecting weaker tax revenue from slower growth and higher welfare spending.

The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the deficit to fall to 2.6% by 2027 if growth accelerates and tax receipts rise, but this assumes no new fiscal shocks and no recessions that would widen the deficit again.

With the 10-year gilt yield at 4.43%, bond investors are pricing in higher structural deficits, because previous gilt auctions in early 2026 saw demand weaken as investors feared debt sustainability if growth disappoints.
expert: The deficit at 4% of GDP masks a structural element, because cyclical unemployment is minimal yet the deficit persists, implying the primary deficit (excluding interest) sits around 2%, driven by welfare spending near 12% of GDP (above OECD average of 11%).

The debt-to-GDP ratio now exceeds 100% and gilt issuance for March-May 2026 is running 15% above previous year levels, while the Bank of England's gilt holdings peaked at 38% of outstanding stock and are now declining at GBP 100bn annually, creating a structural demand gap.

Monitor the May fiscal statement and Q1 2026 tax receipt data (due June) for the inflation surprise signal, because if nominal growth comes in below 3% (implying real growth below 1.5% plus inflation below 1.5%), the OBR will revise the structural deficit to 4.5% and gilt yields will test 4.8%.

beginner: Britain imports 2.5% more goods and services than it exports, which means the country is borrowing from foreigners to pay for what it buys from abroad.
This deficit reflects the fact that British companies aren't exporting enough to cover the cost of imported fuel, food, and manufactured goods, so we rely on foreign investment to balance the books.
If this deficit widens further, the pound could fall, which makes imports more expensive and pushes inflation up, forcing the Bank of England to keep rates high.
moderate: The 2.5% current account deficit is smaller than the pre-2020 average of 3.8%, but has widened from the 2023 low of 1.2%, reflecting stronger import demand as consumer spending recovered while export growth lagged.

Services exports (financial services, consulting, media) have held up well at 15% of GDP, but goods exports remain 8% below 2019 levels due to Brexit trade friction and lower overseas investment in UK manufacturing.

Financing this deficit requires a net inflow of foreign direct investment of around GBP 85bn annually, but FDI has been declining since 2022, creating currency pressure that explains some of GBP/USD weakness.
expert: The current account at minus 2.5% of GDP comprises a goods deficit of 6.5% offset partly by services surplus of 3.2%, with primary income (dividends, interest) running at plus 0.8% as offshore UK assets generate returns.

Brexit structural effects now account for roughly 1.5ppts of the goods deficit widening versus 2015-2018 average, per the Bank of England's trade impact studies, while cyclical demand swings explain the remainder as consumption growth outpaced investment.

Watch June 2026 FDI data and quarterly current account releases for the GBP/USD signal, because if the deficit widens to 3% while FDI inflows fall below GBP 60bn, sterling will test 1.27 versus dollar and gilt yields will spike as foreign buying slows.

beginner: The Bank of England's key interest rate sits at 3.25%, which is the price banks charge each other to borrow money overnight and affects mortgage rates, credit card rates, and savings account rates for ordinary people.

The Bank started cutting rates from 5.25% in August 2025, but inflation at 3.2% means cuts are moving slowly, so mortgage payments won't fall much until the Bank gains confidence prices will stay below 2%.

Goldman Sachs expects the rate to fall to 3% by late 2026, which would ease payments for borrowers but also mean savings accounts earn less, so savers lose purchasing power if inflation stays above 2%.
moderate: At 3.25%, the policy rate has fallen 200bps from the peak in August 2025, but remains above the pre-2022 average of 0.5%, reflecting the Bank's caution given sticky inflation at 3.2% and wage growth at 5%.

The Bank has delivered four 25bps cuts in its last four meetings (November 2025 through February 2026), signaling confidence in the inflation trajectory, but March and May decisions are live calls because of flat inflation and tight labor markets.

Forward guidance from Goldman Sachs and market pricing via swaps suggest rates bottom at 2.75-3% by Q4 2026, implying a terminal rate 75bps above the pre-2020 average, reflecting higher structural inflation and a tighter neutral rate.
expert: The policy rate at 3.25% sits 150bps above the Bank's estimated neutral rate of 1.75% (per February 2026 MPC minutes), signaling ongoing monetary restriction despite the cutting cycle that began in August 2025.

Market pricing via OIS curves shows a 65% probability of a 25bps cut in May 2026 and a terminal rate of 2.9% by September 2026, implying 110bps of total cuts from here, but this assumes inflation falls to 2.2% by year-end, a scenario dependent on wage growth falling to 3.5% or below.

Monitor the April CPI print and May wage data (released in April) for the May decision signal, because if core inflation stays above 3% and wage growth above 4.5%, the Bank pauses the cutting cycle at 3% and extends the hold into Q3 2026, compressing gilt duration trading and pushing 10-year yields above 4.6%.

beginner: UK stocks are up 0.9% so far in 2026, which means the market is barely keeping up with the cost of living and hasn't rewarded investors for the risk they're taking.
This weak performance reflects the fact that companies face sticky inflation, high interest rates, and weak economic growth, so profits aren't rising fast enough to attract new investors.
If rates fall as expected later in the year, stock prices could rise faster, but only if companies can prove they can sell more stuff at higher prices without cutting jobs.
moderate: At 0.9%, the FTSE 100's year-to-date gain lags the S&P 500's 5.25% (in USD terms), reflecting the rotation away from UK-heavy financials and energy as investors favor US technology and artificial intelligence exposure.
The underperformance also reflects currency drag, because the pound has weakened from 1.36 in January to 1.32 in March, so UK stocks in dollar terms have gained 5.25%, masking the domestic weakness.

Valuation metrics show FTSE 100 trading at 13x forward earnings versus historical average of 14x, suggesting limited upside until earnings growth accelerates, which requires either rate cuts to boost activity or a surprise productivity shock.
expert: FTSE 100 at 0.9% YTD masks a bifurcation, large-cap oil and mining stocks (Shell, HSBC, Glencore) have gained 6-8% while mid-cap industrials and housebuilders (Barratt, Spirax-Sarco) have fallen 8-12%, reflecting divergent cycle views on rates and growth.

In GBP terms, the index is essentially flat, but in USD terms (5.25% gain per your data) the appreciation reflects 4.35ppts of currency gain from GBP/USD weakness, not equity alpha, so UK equity risk premium has expanded as foreign capital rotates out.

Watch April earnings season (results released late April and May) for the May rate decision signal, because if FTSE 100 companies guide down 2026 earnings by more than 3% due to demand weakness, equity volatility will spike and 10-year gilt yields will fall as rate cut odds rise above 70% for May.

beginner: UK government bonds maturing in 10 years yield 4.43%, which means investors demand compensation for holding a bond that could lose value if inflation rises or if the pound weakens.

This yield is high enough that some investors prefer bonds to stocks because they don't need growth to go up, they just need the government to pay interest, but it also signals concern about future inflation or deficits.
If the Bank cuts rates and inflation falls as expected, bond yields should fall and existing bond holders will make money, so early 2026 is a good time to own bonds if you think rates will fall.
moderate: At 4.43%, the 10-year gilt yield sits 105bps above the equivalent German Bund (3.38%), reflecting both higher UK inflation at 3.2% versus eurozone 2.3% and a premium for the wider UK fiscal deficit at 4% of GDP.

The yield has stabilized after spiking from 3.8% in November 2025 following the Office for Budget Responsibility's inflation warning, suggesting investors have priced in the current rate cut trajectory and wider deficits.

Curve positioning shows the 2-10 spread at 72bps (steep by recent standards), implying market confidence in the rate-cutting cycle, but if inflation shocks higher or gilt issuance needs rise further, the yield could spike to 4.7% and invert the curve.
expert: The 10-year gilt yield at 4.43% prices in roughly 3bps of term premium relative to the terminal rate of 3% (per Goldman Sachs) plus 40bps of inflation risk premium, implying markets expect inflation to average 2.8% over the 10-year horizon, well above the 2% target.

Gilt issuance through March 2026 reached GBP 105bn, on pace for GBP 145bn for the fiscal year (versus GBP 120bn in FY2024-25), while Bank of England gilt holdings have declined GBP 85bn year-to-date, creating structural supply pressure that explains some of the 4.43% yield level.

Monitor gilt auction results in April-May and the May inflation data for the terminal yield signal, because if issuance exceeds GBP 155bn and inflation prints above 3.5%, gilt yields will push to 4.7% and invert the curve below 2-year rates, signaling recession risk premia and forcing the Bank to pause cuts at 3.25%.

beginner: The difference between short-term and long-term UK interest rates is 72bps, which means investors expect rates to fall over the next decade, so borrowing money long-term is cheaper than borrowing short-term.
This steep curve signals that the market trusts the Bank of England to bring inflation down and cut rates, which is good for people with fixed-rate mortgages because rates won't stay high forever.
